title: Heat-Linked Gene Variant Helps Male Malaria Mosquitoes Mate, May Aid Transmission
excerpt: A Cell study of Anopheles stephensi, the urban malaria vector native to South Asia, finds a deletion in the timeless clock gene gives males a mating edge in high heat while leaving females easier for the malaria parasite to infect.
body:
• A study published in Cell on November 19 finds that a naturally occurring 5-kilobase deletion in the timeless circadian-clock gene gives male Anopheles stephensi mosquitoes a mating advantage in high heat, while making females more susceptible to malaria parasites.
  • Males carrying one copy of the variant achieved 3.6 to 4.7 times higher mating success than ordinary males under high-temperature conditions, and the variant's frequency rose over three generations in semi-field summer experiments.
  • Females carrying the variant showed higher parasite levels in the midgut and substantially higher loads of sporozoites — the parasite stage passed to humans in a bite — in their salivary glands.
  • Anopheles stephensi is the urban malaria mosquito native to South Asia that has spread into Africa since 2012. The study changes no prevention guidance; its authors propose the variant as a marker for tracking how mosquito populations adapt as temperatures rise.

A single genetic variant can make a malaria mosquito better at reproducing in the heat and, at the same time, better at carrying the malaria parasite. That is the finding of a study published in the journal Cell on November 19 by researchers at the Center for Excellence in Molecular Plant Sciences (CEMPS) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, who traced the effect to a naturally occurring deletion in a core circadian-clock gene.

Why this mosquito matters

Malaria parasites are transmitted to people through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes, and the disease remains one of the world's deadliest infections, with an estimated 282 million cases and 610,000 deaths in 2024, according to figures cited in the study report. Among the mosquito species that carry it, Anopheles stephensi draws particular concern: it is native to South Asia and parts of the Arabian Peninsula, breeds readily in human-made water storage containers in cities, tolerates extremely high temperatures, and has been expanding into Africa since it was first detected in Djibouti in 2012.

For India, where An. stephensi is an established urban malaria vector, and for the African cities it is now colonizing, the practical question is how this species adapts as temperatures rise — and whether that adaptation changes its ability to transmit malaria. The CEMPS team, led by Wang Sibao, set out to examine the genetics behind the mosquito's tolerance of heat.

A mating edge for males in the heat

The researchers found a naturally occurring deletion of about 5 kilobases in the timeless (tim) gene, a core component of the insect circadian clock. Its effects depended on both sex and temperature. Mosquitoes with two copies of the deletion showed disrupted daily activity rhythms and reduced mating success. Males with one copy, however, gained a pronounced advantage under high-temperature conditions, achieving 3.6 to 4.7 times higher mating success than wild-type males; the advantage was much less evident at standard temperatures.

Mating-competition experiments using fluorescently labeled sperm confirmed the edge, and in semi-field experiments run over a summer, the frequency of the one-copy genotype and of the variant itself increased across three consecutive generations by more than neutral genetic drift would predict — evidence, the authors say, that the variant can spread through a population when conditions are hot. Mechanistically, the variant stabilized expression of the per clock gene in males at high temperature, raising expression of a hormone gene involved in energy mobilization and flight (AKH1) and of two genes (FAR3 and FAR5) tied to producing heptacosane, a cuticular hydrocarbon used in mating communication.

The same variant weakens females' defenses

In females, the effect ran the other way. Females carrying one copy of the deletion were significantly more susceptible to malaria parasite infection than wild-type females. Infection experiments showed higher parasite prevalence and intensity in the midgut and substantially higher loads of Plasmodium sporozoites in the salivary glands — the parasite stage that is transmitted to a person during a bite. Gene-expression analysis pointed to a cause: reduced expression of antimalarial immune genes, including LRIM15 and PGRP-LD, and experiments that suppressed either gene increased parasite burdens.

The result is a genetic link, not previously recognized, between adaptation to heat and the traits that govern transmission: the variant that helps males win mates in hot weather is inherited by daughters whose defenses against the parasite are weaker.

What it means — and what it does not

The study is basic research, and it changes nothing about day-to-day malaria prevention. Its practical contribution, the authors argue, is surveillance: naturally occurring timeless variants have been identified in both laboratory-selected and wild populations, so the variant could serve as a molecular marker for monitoring how An. stephensi populations are adapting as their range expands and temperatures climb. For control programs — including in Indian cities where this species breeds in overhead tanks and construction-site water — tracking the mosquito's genetics may become as important as tracking its spread. The full study, "A natural mutation of timeless enhances mosquito thermal adaptation and malaria parasite transmission," is available from Cell (DOI: 10.1016/j.cell.2026.10.049), and a summary is carried by Phys.org.
